standard.title: Measure with informal units
standard.description: measure and compare objects based on length, capacity and mass using appropriate uniform informal units and smaller units for accuracy when necessary
standard.prior_knowledge: Students order and compare objects by length, mass and capacity using direct comparison and a single informal unit (AC9M1M01, AC9M1M02). They have not yet justified unit choice, compared multiple units, or used smaller units for greater accuracy.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students measure and compare objects using appropriate uniform informal units across length, capacity and mass, selecting smaller units when greater accuracy is required and explaining their reasoning.

nodes.label: Uniform informal units
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why the informal unit used for measurement must be uniform (identical) and demonstrate what happens when non-uniform units are used.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure the same object with two different-sized informal units; compare results; explain why the units must be the same.
nodes.typical_width: Measure objects using uniform informal units across length, capacity and mass; explain why uniformity matters; demonstrate what goes wrong when units differ (e.g. different shoe sizes give different measurements of the same distance).
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' use of body parts (e.g. hands) as uniform informal units; discuss how a standard unit is maintained when different people measure
Investigate First Nations Australians' use of body measurement to understand animal behaviour: e.g. measuring length, width and depth of animal tracks
nodes.hinge_reason: All measurement activity in Nodes 2 and 3 depends on students understanding why unit uniformity is non-negotiable. Students who accept any same-type unit regardless of size will produce measurements in Nodes 2 and 3 that are meaningless — they cannot compare results across objects or justify unit choice.

response_modes.reason: The need for uniformity is not obvious — students often accept any same-type unit without noticing size differences. Demonstrating failure cases (non-uniform units produce different counts) and then success cases (uniform units produce consistent counts) across multiple contexts makes the principle visible.

success_criteria: Explains that the informal unit must be the same size/mass for measurement to be valid
Demonstrates or explains what goes wrong when non-uniform units are used

nodes.label: Measuring and comparing across attributes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can measure and compare objects using appropriate informal units for length, capacity and mass, counting units and recording results.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure at least one object using informal units for each attribute (length, capacity, mass); count the units; compare two objects for one attribute.
nodes.typical_width: Measure and compare a range of objects using appropriate informal units for length (shorter/longer), capacity (holds more/less) and mass (heavier/lighter); count units; record results; justify unit choice.
wider: Compare the capacity of several containers using sand and a spoon or cup; record results; explain the measurement process including why smaller units give more accurate comparisons
Use balance scales to compare the mass of several objects; count informal units; explain why the unit chosen must have the same mass
success_criteria: Measures an object using informal units for at least two different attributes
Compares two objects for an attribute and states which is longer/heavier/holds more

nodes.label: Smaller units for accuracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why a smaller informal unit gives greater accuracy and choose a smaller unit when more precision is needed.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure one object using a large informal unit; re-measure using a smaller unit; explain why the smaller unit gives a more accurate result.
nodes.typical_width: Choose suitable informal units for measuring a range of objects; justify why a shorter unit suits shorter objects or when more accuracy is needed; explain why a smaller unit produces a larger count.
wider: Measure the same length with three different informal units of different sizes; record all three counts; discuss the inverse relationship between unit size and count
Investigate: can you be more accurate with a smaller unit? Measure a short object with a large unit and a small unit; compare and explain

response_modes.reason: The counterintuitive relationship between unit size and count (smaller unit → larger count for the same length) is a reliable confusion point. Students need to encounter this across multiple measurement contexts — length, capacity, mass — before it generalises.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The inverse relationship between unit size and count is a foundational measurement concept with genuine connections to division, fractions and later work with formal units. Advancing students can articulate this as a principle and apply it to predict relative counts.
success_criteria: Explains that a smaller informal unit gives a more accurate measurement
Explains why a smaller unit produces a larger count for the same object
Chooses an appropriate unit size for a given measurement task and justifies the choice
